neighbours.label: characters inside real base64-encoded text (a blob that decodes to readable data, peaking on the digit '2'); not hex hashes, UUIDs or random key strings
fire: Send the header as Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNzd29yZA== and the server should accept it.
Decoding SGVsbG8gV29ybGQ= gives you the classic string "Hello World".
The JWT payload segment eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwibmFtZSI6IkpvaG4gRG9lIiwiaWF0IjoxNTE2MjM5MDIyfQ holds the subject and the issued-at time.
Embed the icon inline with src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmci" to skip one request.
In the Kubernetes secret, the value field reads c2VjcmV0, which is just the word "secret" encoded.
The tutorial shows that VGhlIHF1aWNrIGJyb3duIGZveA== decodes to "The quick brown fox".
A transparent pixel can be written as data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mNkYPhfDwAChwGA60e6kgAAAABJRU5ErkJggg== in your CSS.
Run echo Zm9vYmFy | base64 -d and the terminal prints foobar.
quiet: Send the header as Authorization: Bearer with your username and password, and the server should accept it.
The SHA-256 checksum of the file is 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824.
Each record gets an ID like 3f2b8c1e-92d4-4a7b-b2e1-0c5d7f9a2e64 when it is created.
Embed the icon inline as an SVG element to skip one extra network request.
In the Kubernetes secret, the value field holds the database password for staging.
The router's MAC address is 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E according to the label.
Run the decode command and the terminal prints the original text back.

predictions: Expect most fire sentences to light the pole (longer blobs best); hex and UUID near misses stay low, though the UUID may leak a little.
